title: The Winter of Cold Spring
premise: Orsen Kavanagh, a meticulous property surveyor, takes a routine appraisal of his late grandmother's house in Cold Spring and finds the inventory wrong: every photograph now contains an extra chair, and the house's measurements refuse to stay constant. As he digs into his grandmother's papers, he learns she made a bargain decades ago—inviting something in to protect her family from a worse truth—and that the invitation transfers by blood. Orsen must decide whether to honor the loyalty that kept his family safe or expose what was invited in, holding out through one long night until sunrise forces the reckoning; he survives by naming the thing aloud at dawn, breaking the inheritance but losing the house, his records, and any certainty about which family stories were ever true.
about_author: I. M. Ravensworth is the pen name of a former land registry clerk who spent fifteen years cataloguing deeds for houses no one would buy twice. They write horror about paperwork, property lines, and the things that sign their names beside ours.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Orsen arrives at his grandmother's Cold Spring house to appraise it for probate, methodically measuring rooms and counting doors. His POV establishes his compulsive precision as comfort. He notes the house measures two feet longer inside than out—an error he assumes is his own. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional routine.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Things
chapters.summary: Cataloguing contents, Orsen photographs each room for the estate file. Reviewing the images that night, he finds every photograph of the parlor includes a wooden chair that wasn't there when he shot it. His POV. Beat: rationalization cracking against evidence he can't delete away.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Orsen returns to verify, counting eleven doors where blueprints show ten. The extra door is painted shut, warm to the touch. A neighbor, Mrs. Aldous, watches him from her porch and says only, 'Your grandmother kept it locked.' His POV. Beat: first confirmation he isn't imagining it.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Searching the attic, Orsen finds his grandmother's ledgers—decades of nightly entries recording the chair's position, the door's temperature, and a single recurring line: 'It has not asked yet.' His POV. Beat: dread shifting from the house to his grandmother's fear.

chapters.title: The Aldous Account
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous, POV shift, recalls 1974: a night when the Kavanagh family faced ruin and scandal, after which they were inexplicably protected and the house was never again sold. She warns Orsen that protection 'comes furnished.' Beat: the town knows more than it says, and loyalty has kept it silent.

chapters.title: Two Feet Longer
chapters.summary: Orsen re-measures the house professionally; the interior discrepancy has grown to six feet, all of it behind the painted door. In the new space, faintly, he hears furniture being arranged. His POV. Beat: the house is not haunted—it is occupied.

chapters.title: The Photographs Change Again
chapters.summary: New photos show the chair moved closer to the camera in each successive frame, as if someone sits down nearer every time Orsen looks. He burns the prints; the negatives reappear in his briefcase. His POV. Beat: surveillance—he is being watched back.

chapters.title: Bloodwork
chapters.summary: In the ledger's final pages, Orsen finds a deed amendment naming 'the seated party' as co-owner, signed in his grandmother's hand and countersigned in a script that matches his own. His POV. Beat: the inheritance isn't money—it's obligation, already transferred.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Recants
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV: she tries to tell Orsen the full story of 1974 but finds herself physically unable to speak the name involved, her mouth filling with cold air. She gives him a key instead—his grandmother's spare, iron, older than the house. Beat: the truth is literally unspeakable; objects must carry it.

chapters.title: Behind the Painted Door
chapters.summary: Using the iron key, Orsen opens the eleventh door onto a room identical to the parlor, furnished entirely with chairs—one for every member of his family tree, each labeled in pencil. One chair is empty, labeled ORSEN. His POV. Beat: the horror of predestination rendered as furniture.

chapters.title: The First Knock
chapters.summary: Night falls early. Something knocks politely at the front door—the rhythm of his grandmother's old greeting knock. Orsen keeps the lights on and does not answer, reciting the inventory aloud to steady himself. His POV. Beat: siege begins; courtesy as menace.

chapters.title: Invited In
chapters.summary: Through the window, Orsen sees the figure on the porch wearing his grandmother's coat, holding a casserole dish like a neighbor come to call. It doesn't force the door. It waits to be let in, because it always has been. His POV. Beat: the realization that hospitality was the trap.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Reading by lamplight, Orsen finds the entry dated the night before his grandmother's death: 'It has asked. I said the boy would answer.' His POV, hands shaking. Beat: betrayal braided with love—she bought time with his name.

chapters.title: Cold Spring Remembers
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV: she gathers three other elderly neighbors who each owe the house a debt, revealing that half the town's prosperity traces to bargains struck in that parlor. They debate warning Orsen versus protecting the arrangement. Beat: justice outside the law—the town polices its own secret.

chapters.title: The Chair Sits Down
chapters.summary: Past midnight, Orsen hears the empty chair in the hidden room scrape across the floor. When he looks, someone is sitting in it—a shape wearing his posture, learning his habits. His POV. Beat: identity theft as haunting; the thing is rehearsing being him.

chapters.title: Terms of the House
chapters.summary: The voice through the door finally speaks, offering the same deal his grandmother took: protection, prosperity, silence—in exchange for the chair staying occupied forever. Orsen demands to know what happened in 1974 before he'll consider anything. His POV. Beat: negotiation; the reader learns the stakes are moral, not just mortal.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: The house itself answers, flooding Orsen with the memory: his grandfather killed a man on the property line and buried him under the parlor; the thing beneath offered concealment, and grandma accepted. Every blessing since grew from that buried crime. His POV. Beat: the theme lands—loyalty to family built on an unexpiated wrong.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Dawn is two hours off. Orsen weighs accepting the bargain—his grandmother did, the town did, everyone he respects did—against exposing the burial and letting the man under the floor be found. The shape in the chair begins speaking in his voice. His POV. Beat: darkest hour; temptation framed as love.

chapters.title: The Uninviting
chapters.summary: Orsen understands the rule at last: the thing can only hold what is invited and unnamed. He opens the front door himself, faces his grandmother's coat, and speaks the buried man's name aloud—the one fact no ledger recorded. The house convulses. His POV. Beat: climax; truth as exorcism.

chapters.title: Sunrise Inventory
chapters.summary: As light enters, the chairs topple one by one, the eleventh door seals into plain wall, and the extra two feet collapse inward with a sound like a held breath released. The shape in the chair unravels mid-gesture, still wearing Orsen's face. His POV. Beat: catharsis through destruction.

chapters.title: Probate
chapters.summary: Weeks later, surveyors find human remains beneath the parlor; the Kavanagh name is dragged through the papers Orsen files himself, refusing anonymity. Mrs. Aldous and the neighbors shun him—but one young Aldous thanks him quietly. Orsen's POV. Beat: justice outside the law fulfilled at personal cost.

chapters.title: The Last Appraisal
chapters.summary: Orsen appraises the emptied house one final time for demolition, measuring rooms that now match their blueprints exactly. In the last photograph he takes, there is no chair at all—only sunlight on bare floorboards. He locks the door behind him and does not count them. His POV. Beat: resolution; peace purchased by giving up the comfort of certainty.
